tagline.text: A quiet peninsula with a 130-year-old lighthouse and sandbars

children.text: The Calatagan Peninsula stretches out at the western tip of Batangas, between the South China Sea and Balayan Bay. It suits travelers looking for a quiet beach trip, with a Spanish-era lighthouse built in 1890, Burot Beach where you can pitch a tent for the night, and sandbars and over-water cottages that appear at low tide.

Calatagan is a coastal town occupying the Calatagan Peninsula, which stretches south from the western tip of Batangas province. The South China Sea (West Philippine Sea) lies to the west, Balayan Bay to the east, and the southern tip meets the mouth of the Verde Island Passage between Mindoro and Luzon. It's about
from Manila, a
3–4-hour
drive, but it's less developed than neighboring Nasugbu or Lian, so you can enjoy a relatively quiet sea even on weekends.
At Santiago Point, on the peninsula's southwestern tip, stands the Cape Santiago Lighthouse, completed by the Spanish colonial government in
. It's a round tower of red brick standing about

tall, with input from Magin Pers y Pers, who also designed the Cape Bojeador Lighthouse in Ilocos. It's still an active lighthouse guiding ships through the Verde Island Passage today, one of the longest continuously operating lighthouses in the Philippines.

Calatagan is also known for archaeology. In the 1950s, a large number of pre-colonial pottery pieces and Chinese ceramics were excavated from old graves here, revealing that a large settlement once stood here and traded directly with China. The "Calatagan pot" found at that time bears markings believed to be the ancient Philippine script baybayin; it has been declared a national cultural treasure and is now on display at the National Museum in Manila. In the 20th century, a large sugarcane plantation run by the Zobel family brought wide pastures and vacation estates to parts of the peninsula.

For travelers, Calatagan is a place for "a quiet sea and camping." The sand runs from white to cream, and wide seagrass beds spread across the shallow water, exposing sandbars and tide pools at low tide. It suits a restful trip over a party trip, friends who love tents and barbecues, and anyone who wants to photograph the lighthouse and sunset.

A brick lighthouse over 130 years old still stands, along with the red-roofed former keeper's quarters. The sunset viewed from the rocky shore behind the lighthouse is beautiful, and inside the keeper's quarters are rooms that hint at how it once looked.

A quiet beach northwest of the lighthouse, a popular spot for pitching a tent and spending the night. Electricity and amenities are limited, which only makes the stars easier to see. Operations and fees change from time to time, so check before you go.
Renting a bamboo cottage built on stilts in the shallow water and spending the day there is a Calatagan specialty. At low tide, sandbars appear around the cottages so you can walk between them.
A short resort-boat tour visits sandbars that appear only at low tide, a shallow island thick with starfish, and a white sand islet known as "Little Boracay." The route changes with the tide.
At the Calatagan Mangrove Forest Protected Park, bamboo walkways let you stroll through the mangroves and spot crabs, mudskippers, and waterbirds. It makes a good nature-learning stop with children.
The shallow water around the peninsula has seagrass beds and small coral patches where starfish, sea urchins, and small fish are easy to spot. It suits light snorkeling more than diving.

children.text: The small town center, with its town plaza and Santo Domingo Church, and the wide pastures and horse ranches at the heart of the peninsula, show a side of Calatagan quite different from its beaches.

The sandbars and over-water cottages depend on the tide. Check a tide table before you go, and schedule them for the afternoon of Day 1 or the morning of Day 2.
Buses and vans to Calatagan run from southern Manila terminals such as Pasay Buendia (near LRT's Gil Puyat station), operated by companies like DLTB. It takes about
3–4 hours
, for around
, and drops you off in front of Calatagan's public market.
If there's no direct trip to Calatagan, take one bound for Nasugbu or Balayan and transfer to a jeepney to Calatagan. The last trip tends to be early, so check your return time in advance.
Take SLEX or CAVITEX up to Tagaytay, head down the Tagaytay–Nasugbu Highway, then go through Palico junction and Lian to reach Calatagan. Without traffic it takes about
3 hours–3 hours 30 minutes
The coastal route along Cavite through the Ternate–Nasugbu road (Kaybiang Tunnel) is scenic but has many winding mountain sections, so use it only if you're confident driving.
From Calatagan market to the lighthouse takes about
20–30 minutes
by tricycle, for about
per trip. Beach resorts and Burot Beach cost about the same to reach.
The lighthouse and beaches are remote, so it can be hard to flag down a tricycle for the return trip. Get the driver's phone number, or agree on a waiting fee and use the same tricycle round trip.
The
December–May
season, when the northeast monsoon (Amihan) blows, is best. The mountains shelter the peninsula's western coast from the wind, so the sea is calm and skies are clear on many days. Locals rate
January–February
highest, when it's less crowded and not too hot;
March–May
is clearest of all, but midday temperatures climb to
, and resorts get crowded during Holy Week and summer break.
June–October

is the rainy season, when the southwest monsoon (Habagat) blows straight in from the western sea, bringing high waves and frequent rain to Calatagan's west coast. Tent camping and island hopping become nearly impossible, and beachfront resorts sometimes close when a typhoon hits. During this period, it's better to pick a clear day and keep the trip short, focused on the lighthouse and the mangrove forest.
Prices are approximate as of
and may vary depending on local conditions.
Calatagan's lodging falls into three broad types: campsites for pitching a tent, like Burot Beach; beach resorts with simple cottages and rooms (about
per night); and larger resorts with pools and over-water cottages (about

). Stilts Calatagan Beach Resort, long popular for its over-water cottages and sandbar tours, is a well-known option, and simpler beach resorts also accept guests who just pay an entrance fee to spend the day. Cottages and rooms fill up fast on peak-season weekends, so book ahead.

There aren't many beachfront restaurants, so it's common to buy fish, squid, pork, and vegetables at Calatagan's public market and grill them yourself at your resort or campsite. Batangas specialties like bulalo (beef bone-marrow soup), Batangas lomi, sinaing na tulingan (braised tuna), and strong kapeng barako coffee are worth trying in Balayan, Nasugbu, or Tagaytay along the way. If you're camping, bring plenty of water and ice.
Sandbars and island hopping depend on low tide. Check a tide table and plan your trip for a day when low tide falls during daylight hours.
There are almost no convenience stores or ATMs near the beaches. Take care of cash and groceries in Calatagan town or a larger town along the way.
If you're camping, bring a tent, a lantern, insect repellent, and a power bank. Electricity and shower facilities at campsites are limited.
The lighthouse looks best at sunset. Closing time tends to be early, so check the operating hours and arrive by
4 PM
at the latest.
Sea urchins are common in the seagrass beds and tide pools. Wear aqua shoes, and only look at creatures like starfish — don't pick them up.
Many resorts charge extra for bringing in outside food. Before you go shopping, check the policy and the grill rental fee.
Stopping in Tagaytay on the way back lets you end the trip with cool air, a view of Taal Volcano, and a bowl of bulalo.
Sandbars submerge quickly once the tide starts coming in. If you've walked far out at low tide, head back before the water rises, and keep a close eye on children.
The lighthouse tower and the old keeper's quarters are historic heritage structures. Don't write on the walls or enter restricted areas.
Campsites and small resorts often have no lifeguard. Swim only during the day, and never after drinking.
The interior of the peninsula has extensive private land and pasture. Don't enter posted private property, and stick to marked roads.
Carry your beach trash back out with you. Use the trash bags provided at the campsite, and don't light fires on the seagrass beds.
Waves on the west coast get very high during the rainy and typhoon season. Skip swimming and boat tours when there's a weather advisory.
